justification_text:
My point estimates across all three horizons sit close to 49–49.5, reflecting a near-neutral baseline assumption. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 48.9 is essentially anchored to the most recent observed value with minimal drift expected over such a short window. The slight upward drift as we move to one week (49.1) and one month (49.5) reflects a weak mean-reversion or slight positive drift assumption built into the model, acknowledging that if the current reading is slightly below a long-run equilibrium, there is mild upward pressure over time. None of these point estimates represent a strong directional conviction — they are more a reflection of "expect things to remain roughly where they are" with a marginal tilt.

The confidence interval widths expand substantially as the horizon lengthens, which is the natural consequence of uncertainty compounding over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 1.8 units on either side, reflecting relatively tight short-term predictability — most noise that could affect the value within a single day is bounded and well-characterized. By one week, the interval widens to roughly 3.3 units on either side, incorporating the possibility of moderate news shocks, data revisions, or shifting sentiment. At one month, the interval opens to about 6.5 units on either side, acknowledging that over a 30-day window, macroeconomic releases, policy shifts, geopolitical developments, and structural changes in underlying conditions can all push the value meaningfully away from where it started.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside the stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected deterioration in macroeconomic conditions — such as a surprise contraction in activity data, an adverse central bank announcement, or a geopolitical shock — could drive the value below 43 at the one-month horizon. On the upside, stronger-than-expected fundamental data, a policy pivot toward stimulus, or a broad improvement in risk appetite could push the value above 56. These tail scenarios are assigned low but non-trivial probability precisely because such events, while uncommon in any given month, are recurring features of real-world dynamics.

It is also worth noting that the intervals assume relatively stable volatility regimes. If conditions shift into a high-volatility environment — for instance, during a financial stress episode or a rapid escalation in geopolitical tensions — realized outcomes could land well outside even the stated 90% bounds. Conversely, in a particularly calm and low-information environment, actual outcomes might cluster much more tightly than the intervals suggest. The stated confidence intervals are best interpreted as reflecting typical uncertainty under moderate conditions, not as hard limits.
